# Conductor

> Run graphs of typed Python functions.

A node is a function whose typed signature is its interface. A graph is data, a graph record: its nodes, each with its constants, and the edges between their outputs and inputs. `Graph.compile(record, registry)` makes a `Graph` that reports what is wrong; a `Graph` runs, calling a node once per item wherever it is wired to a series (a list a node returns as `Series[T]`), and a run is one value, `Run`, that pauses for a person, resumes and writes itself as JSON. The host declares its own types and nodes.

## Quick Start

One node returns many values, one takes a single value, one takes them all; that is all iteration is.

```python
registry = NodeRegistry()


@registry.node("lines", title="Lines", description="The lines of a text.")
def lines(text: str) -> Series[str]:
    return text.splitlines()


@registry.node("upper", title="Uppercase", description="Turns a text into capital letters.")
def upper(text: str) -> str:
    return text.upper()


@registry.node("join", title="Join", description="Joins every text it is given.")
def join(texts: Series[str]) -> str:
    """Joins every text it is given."""
    return "+".join(texts)


assert upper("a") == "A"  # a node is called like its function

graph = Graph.compile(GraphRecord.model_validate({            # a graph is data: a GraphRecord, or its JSON text
    "nodes": [{"id": "lines", "node": "lines"}, {"id": "upper", "node": "upper"}, {"id": "join", "node": "join"}],
    "edges": [["lines.result", "upper.text"], ["upper.result", "join.texts"]],
}), registry)
assert graph.is_runnable, graph.problems

run = graph.run(text="a\nb\nc")    # by address: graph.run({"lines.text": ...})
run.outputs                        # {"join.result": "A+B+C"}: what the graph returns, by address
run.results["upper"]["result"]     # ["A", "B", "C"]: ran once per item of lines.result
run.results["join"]["result"]      # "A+B+C": Series[str] received every value, once
```

`make_graph(*nodes, edges=None, constants={}, defaults={})` writes a `GraphRecord`, each node at its version and under its own id (`upper-1`, `upper-2` when one is used twice). With no `edges` the nodes form a chain: each takes its one required input that has no constant from the one output of the node before it (`not_a_chain` otherwise). A chain reads the fields each node declares; a subgraph, or a node whose fields a hook works out, takes `edges=`. With `edges=[("upper.result", "join.texts")]` those are every edge; nothing is matched by name. `constants={"upper.text": "x"}` gives inputs constants, the same on every call of every run; `defaults=` gives values the caller may change. `make_graph` writes the record and compiles nothing. It raises one `InvalidCallError` listing what it can't write: a value or default addressed to a node it wasn't given (`node_not_in_graph`), a value with no JSON form or with a set in it (`invalid_value`), an edge that is no address (`invalid_record`), a chain it can't draw (`not_a_chain`). Everything else (an input or output a node doesn't have, a value its field refuses, a default no caller reaches, an edge between types that don't meet, a graph half drawn) is in `Graph.compile(record, registry).problems`.

## Core Concepts

### The Node Contract

`@node("id", version=, title=, description=, category=, tags=, extra=, docs=, policy=, deprecation=, compute_added_inputs=, compute_outputs=, replaces=, upgrade=)` wraps a plain function and returns a frozen, callable `FunctionDefinition`; it registers nothing. `subgraph("id", title=, description=, ...)(record)` makes a `SubgraphDefinition`, which has no function, so calling it is a type error; `NodeDefinition` is the union of the two, and a reader tells them apart with `match`. `@registry.node(...)` takes the same arguments and adds the node to that registry. The id, `title` and `description` are required, and an empty `title` or `description` (or one of only spaces) is a `NodeDeclarationError` of `empty_title_or_description`: the title and description are what a person reads for the node, and the docstring is the developer's, never shown. A field's label is its name made readable (`case_sensitive` is "Case sensitive") unless its `Param(title=)` says otherwise. `extra` is the host's own JSON about the node, kept and described, never read by conductor.

- Input: `text: str`, or `Annotated[str, Param(title=, description=, widget=, ge=, le=, max_length=, ...)]`. Without a widget an editor shows no control for it: an edge fills it, or a value set in code. A default makes it optional, and is checked against the type and written as JSON once, where it is written; one that isn't of its type, or that its type can't write as JSON, is `default_invalid`. A limit that can't apply to its type (`ge` on a `str`) is refused where it is written (`bound_invalid`). Stacked `Param`s (an alias such as `Annotated[str, Param(widget=TextInput())]` wrapped again with `Param(min_length=1)`) merge as pydantic stacks its fields, the later winning per argument and per limit; a `Param` on a `Series` item is the field's.
- Choices: `Param(choices=[...])`, each a value or a `Choice(id, title)` (from `conductor`), is the one home of a field's choices, carried in its record as `choices`: on a `Literal` field they title its values, one each; on any other they limit what it takes (`not_a_choice`). Each is read as an answer is, strictly from its JSON form and held to the field's limits, so an enum's value or a date's ISO text is a choice. With none, a `Literal` field's choices are its values. An `Ask` gives a question choices the run knows; else a question has its output's. Errors: `choices_invalid`.
- Output: `-> str` is one output named `result`, `Annotated[str, Param(title=)]` says more; a frozen dataclass is one output per field, and `Param(exclusive_group=)` on its fields makes them alternatives, branches (at most one has a value on a call, else `invalid_output`); any other type is one value, a `dict[str, int]` included; with `compute_outputs` the function returns the outputs the hook gives as a mapping by name; `-> None` declares no outputs.
- A value can be `None`. An input receives `None` only if its type says so (`email: str | None`, or `Any`); otherwise the node isn't called for that item, its outputs are `None` there (of branches in an `exclusive_group`, none is chosen, so what is wired to either branch is skipped there), and `run.not_called` records the node, the item and the input. `Series[X]` leaves `None` items out and `Series[X | None]` keeps them (see "One or many"). `Series[X] | None` is a list or `None` in place of it, and `Table[R] | None` a table or `None`: `None` given, as a constant or as its default, a node may return `None` for either, and a list or table never returned (its node had a `None` argument, or returned `None`) reaches it as `None`; `Series[X] = None` without `| None` is `default_invalid`.
- A node with one input on a branch not chosen and another `None` is skipped, whatever the order of its parameters: a skip wins over a `None`, and over an input whose edge names a field its record lacks, which fails the call (`invalid_edge_value`, the first such input in the signature) only when no input is skipped. It wins over an input that has no value yet too: the node is skipped at once, and the nodes downstream go on, while the other input's source still waits for a person.
- The function returns `SKIPPED` on a branch not chosen and raises `Ask(...)` when a person must answer, which its `@node` declares with `asks=True`. `Ask` is a `BaseException`, so an `except Exception` in the node lets it through.
- What the host supplies for a run arrives as the run's context, a node's first parameter typed `Context[X]`.
- `@node` checks the function: an `async def`, a parameter with no type, `*args`, `**kwargs` with no `compute_added_inputs`, a dataclass of outputs that isn't frozen, and a field name gone from the next version with no `Upgrade` raise `NodeDeclarationError`, with a `code`.

### Versions and Policies

A newer version names the one it replaces, a `@node` of the same id, and the decorated function is the newest. A definition is one version, and each version names the one before it in `replaces`. The older versions are plain `@node` definitions that are never registered; only the newest goes on a registry, and an id the registry already has is `duplicate_node_id` whatever `replaces=` names (`registry.replace(newer)` swaps a held node).

```python
@node("greet", title="Greet", description="Greets a person by name.")
def greet_v1(name: Annotated[str, Param(title="Name", widget=Textarea())]) -> str:
    return f"Hello {name}"

def _split_name(values: dict) -> dict:
    first, _, last = values.pop("name").partition(" ")
    return {**values, "first": first, "last": last}

@node("greet", title="Greet", description="Greets a person by first and last name.", policy=Policy(retries=2, retry_delay=0.5, attempt_timeout=10, concurrency=4), replaces=greet_v1, upgrade=Upgrade(rewrite=_split_name))
def greet(first: str, last: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello {first} {last}"

assert greet.versions == (2, 1) and greet.version_of(1) is greet_v1
```

- `Policy(concurrency=1, retries=0, retry_delay=1.0, attempt_timeout=None, retry_on=(), reuse_when_inputs_match=True, costs_nothing=False)`. With `concurrency` 1 and no `attempt_timeout` the node is called in order on the run's own thread; otherwise on threads, at most `concurrency` calls at once. `concurrency` is at least 1, `retries` at least 0, `retry_delay` finite seconds of at least 0 and `attempt_timeout` finite seconds above 0; anything else raises pydantic's own validation error, as `Policy` is a pydantic model read strictly: a yes or no, a text or `1.5` is no whole number.
- `version=` is one past the version replaced, or 1; a host whose subgraphs have their own numbers names them. `Upgrade(renamed_inputs={old: new}, renamed_outputs={old: new}, rewrite=fn)` goes beside `replaces=`; an input rename carries its value, default and edges in, an output rename the edges out of it and out of a field of it, and `fn` takes and returns the node's constants and defaults as one dict (a default stays one, anything new is a constant); an edge into an input the new version neither keeps nor renames is dropped. It is required only when a field name of the replaced version is gone: a gone input needs a rename or `fn`, a gone output a rename (`upgrade_missing` at the declaration).
- `registry.upgrade(record, node_id, to=None)` moves one node to a version and returns a `GraphRecord`; what it can't do is `InvalidCallError`. Compiling never upgrades: a graph record that names an old version runs it.
- `Deprecation(header=, description=, alternative=, migration=)` marks a version going away (`deprecation=` on its `@node`). The `alternative` is an id for a person to read.
- A graph record can be a node too, a subgraph: `subgraph("enrich", title="Enrich", description="...")(record)`, with `replaces=` and `version=` as any node, and no `policy` or hook, since its nodes run by their own; `registry.subgraph(...)` takes the same arguments and adds the node. Its inner nodes run inside every loop the subgraph node is inside; from outside it is one node (see "The graph record"), whose inputs are its graph's inputs, by their names there (`text`, `t.text` on a clash), and whose outputs are its graph's outputs, by their addresses there (`t.result`).

### Field Hooks

```python
def operand_inputs(count: int) -> dict:          # inputs to ADD; the function takes them as **values
    return {f"value_{i}": float for i in range(count)}


def branch_outputs(names: str, value: type) -> dict:   # all the outputs; value: the type arriving on "value"
    return {name: Annotated[value, Param(exclusive_group="branches")] for name in names.split(",")}
```

Each is a plain function, given per version (`compute_added_inputs=` and `compute_outputs=` on `@node`), called when a graph is compiled, never per call. A parameter names an input and receives its constant, else the declared default; a parameter annotated `type` receives the type arriving on that input by its edge, `Any` until one does, and `**added: type` on `compute_outputs` receives the type arriving on each input `compute_added_inputs` added. A table arriving is `Table[R]` or a bare `Table`, so `typing.get_args(table)` is its record type `R`, or empty. An input a hook reads is decided when the graph is compiled: it takes a constant or the node's default, is never one of the graph's inputs, and a record default there is `default_not_a_graph_input`. If it has neither a constant nor a default, the hook is not called and the node's own problem says why. A hook returns `{name: type hint}`, read like a signature, or `{name: (type hint, default)}` for a field with a default, as pydantic's `create_model` takes one. A hook that raises is the problem `compute_hook_failed` on the node, never an exception; one that raises `NodeError` gives it its message, its `code` as `ctx.error`, and its own `ctx` whole as `ctx.error_ctx`. `graph.describe()` shows each node's fields as its hooks made them.

### A node for any type

A signature may hold type variables: `def keep[T](value: T) -> T`, `def split[T](value: Table[T] | list[T]) -> Series[T]`, and a frozen dataclass of outputs may be generic too, with one output per field. A variable is what arrives on the edge, in every input and in the return, decided when the graph is compiled; after that the node has ordinary inputs and outputs and its output is checked against the bound type. Only an edge binds: a constant, a default and a graph input bind nothing, and a variable nothing binds reads as its bound (`T: int | float`), else `Any`. One or many is decided first, so a `Series[X]` at `value: T` runs per item with `T` as `X`. In a union the option shaped like the arriving type binds; at `T | None`, `T` is what arrives without its `None`, and at a bare `T` too, so `value: T` receives no `None` (the node isn't called for one) and a node that passes `None` on writes `T | None`; two places for one variable join (`int | str`); what arrives outside a bound is `type_mismatch`. A variable on no input is `type_variable_only_in_return`, a constrained one (`T: (int, str)`) `type_variable_constrained`, both at `@node`. A hook stays for what a type can't say: outputs named by a constant, and a record computed from other records.

### Types

Any type pydantic can check and write as JSON travels on edges: `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `date`, `datetime`, a pydantic model or a dataclass of your own, a `TypedDict` (a record: it names a table's columns, and travels alone as one line of it); a plain class is refused (`type_not_carried`). `Annotated` metadata that is no `Param` is pydantic's: `Annotated[int, annotated_types.Gt(0)]`, pydantic's own `pydantic.PositiveInt` and `constr(min_length=1)` are read as pydantic reads them. Two things there are refused. A widget (`widget_outside_param`) goes on `Param(widget=...)`. Pydantic's `pydantic.Field(...)` (`pydantic_field_in_hint`) is written as `Param`, the one way to give an input or an output its title, description and limits: `Annotated[int, Param(ge=0)]`, never `Annotated[int, pydantic.Field(ge=0)]`, on the parameter, the return type, an item of a `Series`, list or dict, or a column of a table's row type; `pydantic.Field(...)` on the fields of a model or dataclass of your own is that class's, and a union is told apart with `pydantic.Discriminator("kind")`. A subtype lands where its parent is asked for, an `int` lands on a `float`, a `Literal` on a `Literal` holding all its values, and a generic by its arguments too: `list[int]` lands on `list[float]` and never on `list[str]`. A type alias (`type X = ...`, pydantic's JsonValue) is read as what it stands for: text, a number, a yes or no, or a list or dict of them lands on a JsonValue, a model or a date does not, and it takes `None` when what it stands for does. What a person sees for a type is declared, never guessed. Conductor's own types (the builtins, decimals, dates, times, durations, UUIDs, dicts, lists, tuples, sets and `Any`) take their id and title from one fixed table (`str` is titled "Text", `int` "Whole number", `float` "Number", `bool` "Yes or no"). A type of your own on a field or a table's column is declared with `@host_type("money", title="Money", accepts=[...])` above the class (above `@dataclass` when there is one; `host_type("ip", title="IP address")(the_class)` for a library's class): the id is the name an editor and a graph record know it by, the title what a person reads. The declaration is checked when the class statement ends (`type_declaration_invalid`: an id that is not one word or is one of conductor's own, an empty title, `accepts` with something other than classes in it; `type_not_carried`: a class pydantic can't validate), and a class with no declaration fails where its node is declared (`type_not_named`); a subclass declares its own. It is a decorator and not a base class because a base class runs before the class is finished, which breaks a generic pydantic model, `@dataclass(slots=True)` and enums, and a library's class can't be given one. Fields named `id` or `title` stay the record's own. A `TypedDict` declares nothing: its id is `record`, and a table's id names its columns (`Table[name: str, email: str | None]`). A generic is known by its class and arguments (`dict[str, int]`; a bare `list` for `list[Any]`), so a class of your own inside one is declared too, and a generic pydantic model declared as `box` is `box[int]` with an `int` inside; a `Literal` is known by its values' types, a union by its members, a type alias by its name. `accepts=[...]` lists the other classes whose values may land on the type; it reads such a value itself. A subclass of a builtin (`class Text(str)`) needs only its declaration: a value is validated as the builtin and then made the subclass; a class that needs another way gives its own `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`. A yes or no never lands on an `int` or `float` input, nor on a union holding a number and no `bool` (`int | float`, `int | str`), nor on a host's subclass of one whatever its `accepts` says, nor as an item of a list, dict or `Series` of them, by edge (`type_mismatch`), constant (`invalid_value`) or caller (`invalid_input`), nor in a table's `int` or `float` column, returned (`invalid_output`), brought by an edge (`invalid_edge_value`) or given (`invalid_input`).

- `registry.types`: every class its nodes' field types name (each member of a union, a `Literal`'s value types, a generic's class and its arguments'; not `Any`, `None`, a type alias or a table) plus `NodeRegistry(types=[...])`, by id; one id claimed by two classes raises (`duplicate_type_id`). `registry.describe().types[...].accepted_as`: the ids a value of that type may land on.
- `Series[X]`: many values of one type. A plain list to the node and to a type checker; a `polars.Series` returned for one is read as its values, though a checker wants `series.to_list()`. `list[X]` stays one value that is a list.
- `Table[R]`, whose columns a `TypedDict` names (a column's `Param` limits are held), or bare `Table`: a whole table, one value, a `polars.DataFrame` at run time. It is a type like any other: it can be a member of a union (`Table[R] | list[T]`), an item of a `Series` (`Series[Table[R]]`) and a field of a record. A table is read from a frame or from a list of records, one object per row, wherever it comes from (a caller, a person's answer, collected records, a node's own return), and a `Table[R]` has exactly `R`'s columns once read: each present, others cut, so a node that passes columns it doesn't name returns a bare `Table`. A table of no rows has every declared column. As JSON a table is `{"columns": [{"name", "type", "values"}]}`, its columns in order, `type` the word for the cells (`bool`, `int`, `float`, `str`, `date`, `datetime`, `time`, `timedelta`, a decimal as its class name, else `json`): in a default, a waiting call's inputs and a saved run. A column may have a `None` only where its type says `| None`; a table with a `None` in any other column is refused where it arrives, naming the column (`invalid_output`, `invalid_input`, `invalid_edge_value`). To a type checker it is a frame that names `R`: frame methods need no narrowing and a plain `polars.DataFrame` may be returned. A checker shows `R` (`reveal_type`, `assert_type`), but it accepts a table of one record type where another is expected, because the type includes a plain `polars.DataFrame`.

### The graph record

`GraphRecord(nodes=[...], edges=[(from, to), ...])`, stored as `{"nodes": [...], "edges": [["a.result", "b.text"], ...]}`; `NodeRecord(id=, node=, version=1, constants=, defaults=, display=)`, empty fields left out when saved. `constants`, `defaults` and a node's `display` hold JSON values; `make_graph` writes a Python value as its JSON (a date as its ISO text, an enum as its value, a float that isn't finite as its text, `"NaN"` or `"Infinity"`), so a record equals what its JSON reads back; a record built holding a float that isn't finite is refused. A value with no JSON form, such as a `polars.DataFrame` (give a table as a list of records), is `invalid_value` at the call. `node` is the id of the node it uses. A node id is not empty and may not contain `.`, `/`, `@` or `~` (`invalid_node_id`).

- A subgraph is one node. Its inputs are that graph's `graph.inputs`, by their names there (`emb.text`; `emb.x.text` where two inner inputs share a name), and its outputs that graph's `graph.outputs`, by their addresses there, so an author wires `emb.upper.result`. A node outside reads a subgraph's output as it would read the same node drawn in its own graph. For the subgraph `documents -> lines -> shout`, where `shout` is called once per line of each document, an input of one `str` wired to `emb.shout.result` is called once per line, and a `Series[str]` input once per document with that document's lines, the list per document `run.results` shows. A loop outside is named by the list inside that is looped over (`runs_on` says `per item of emb.documents.result`), so two outputs returned in the same loop inside line up: a node that takes one item of each is called once per item with both values, and a node that takes one value per document beside a `Series` of that document's lines is called once per document. Outputs returned in different loops inside don't line up (`series_not_nested`, `ctx.variant` `inside_subgraph`, which says to give one whole to a `Series` input or return both from the same loop inside). The description of such an output says `is_series` with one `Series` per loop (`type` `Series[str]` for `Series[Series[str]]`) and lists its `loops` by their addresses inside, `["documents.result", "lines.result"]`; `loops` is empty for every other field. A `Series` returned once per document is `Series[Series[T]]` the same way, and a table returned once per document a `Series` of tables. An exclusive group inside is named by its deciding node, `d.answer`. Two outputs that depend on opposite branches of one decision inside are alternatives outside, as the same nodes drawn in the outer graph are: both may be wired into one input, and each call gets the value from the branch that was chosen (and collected into two `Series` inputs of one node they are `lists_from_different_loops`). An inner input a hook reads is set inside the subgraph and is not offered. A subgraph is compiled once, alone, so a type variable at one of its graph inputs has no edge to bind it and reads as its bound, else `Any`: a subgraph whose first node is `series-split` offers `Table | list` and gives records of unknown fields, where the same nodes drawn in the graph would have the arriving table's. A first node whose input has a precise type (`Table[R]`, `R` a `TypedDict`) gives the subgraph its type. A `Series` input inside a subgraph collects only the loops inside that graph: wired to a value returned once inside, it is a list of one, whatever loop the subgraph node is inside outside. Using a graph as a subgraph changes nothing about how the inner nodes behave: each is called by its own `Policy` (its `concurrency` counts its calls across every item the subgraph's node runs for, its retries and `attempt_timeout` are its own), a cancel and the `timeout` of `resume()` stop them as they stop any node, and `run.again` reuses the previous run's outcomes node by node; the subgraph takes no `Policy`. `results`, `runs_on` and `describe()` show it as one node, whose outputs are the outputs of the inner nodes that return them: it is never called and has no outputs of its own, so a subgraph costs what its nodes cost. It says `node_start` when the first node inside starts and `node_complete` (or `node_skipped`) once every node inside has, with `outcomes` the number of items it runs for, and no `node_progress`. A `None` or a branch not chosen arriving at one of its inputs makes the inner nodes wired to it not called, or skipped, as it would with the same nodes drawn in the graph, and `run.not_called` lists those nodes. What is inside is told with where it is: a problem's `loc` starts with the node and item of each subgraph around it (`("emb", 1, "upper")`; a compile problem of the subgraph is its own problem behind the subgraph node's id, `("emb", "upper", "text")`), a `Waiting` and a `NotCalled` have the same `loc`, and a waiting id spells it `emb@1/ask~3fa2c0d1`. An inner node says its events once, as any node that runs per item does, with the ids of the subgraphs' nodes around it in front, `("emb", "upper")`.
- Edges are a list, kept sorted, so two records differing only in edge order are equal; an edge listed twice stays twice, and compiling reports it (`repeated_edge`). An edge is `node.field`, or `node.output.field` for one field of a record that output gives. Several edges into one input are alternatives (see "One or many"). An edge naming a node the graph doesn't have, at either end, is `edge_names_missing_node`.
- `constants`: the input's value on every call of every run; the graph doesn't offer that input to a caller.
- `defaults`: a value the caller may change. Only a graph input (an input with no edge on a node with no incoming edges) has a caller, so a default elsewhere is `default_not_a_graph_input`: write a constant. An input takes an edge, a value or a default, never two (`constant_and_edge`, `constant_and_default`).
- One value or many: the type decides, never the value. A list (a JSON array, a Python list or tuple) given for, or written as the constant of, an input that takes one value of a type taking no list is refused: `invalid_input` when given, `invalid_value` as a constant. An input whose own type takes a list (`list[str]`, `Series[...]`, `Table[...]`, `Any`) takes the list as one value, and an open `Series` input takes only a list: one value given there is `invalid_input`. A set has no order, so it is never a list: a set given or written as a constant (an upgrade's rewrite included) is refused with `set_has_no_order` in the problem's `errors`, and so is a constant with a set anywhere in it.
- Nothing set: the declared default.
- `display`: the host's own, stored and never read. What a host keeps about the whole graph (a name, a viewport) it stores beside the record.
- A subgraph node's inputs get their values from outside as any node's do: a constant, a default or an edge in the outer graph takes the place of a default in the subgraph's own record.

### Compiling

`Graph.compile(record, registry)` takes a `GraphRecord` or its JSON text; a host that has a dict writes `GraphRecord.model_validate(data)`. JSON text that isn't a record's shape raises `InvalidCallError` of `invalid_record` problems. It never raises for a fault in the graph: each fault is a `Problem` (`type`, `loc`, `msg`, `ctx`) in `graph.problems`, and `graph.is_runnable` says whether there are none.

- The rule: the shape is the call's, what the shape says is the graph's. What doesn't have a record's shape raises `InvalidCallError`, one `invalid_record` problem per fault, at `("record", *where)`, with pydantic's code in `ctx.error`. That covers text that isn't JSON, a key a record doesn't have (`vaules`, or `type` for `node`), a field of the wrong type, and an edge that isn't a pair of addresses.
- The graph keeps its own copy of the definitions it resolved, so a later change to the registry doesn't reach it.
- A graph that uses subgraphs made for one request is compiled with a registry of its own: a new `NodeRegistry`, `add_subregistry(shared)`, then `add(*definitions)`. `docs/subgraphs.md` teaches it.

- `graph.inputs`: the graph inputs, the inputs with no edge on the nodes with no incoming edges (and no hook reads them), by bare name or by address where two share a name. Each is a `GraphInputDescription`: `address`, `node_id` and `field`, the input's `FieldDescription`, whose `default` is the record's default, else the node's, as JSON, `None` when `required`. A graph input with no value yet is not a problem; a required input with no edge on a node that has incoming edges is `unbound_on_later_node`.
- `graph.outputs`: the outputs of the nodes with no outgoing edges, by address. `graph.runs_on`: how often each node runs, a `RunsOn` whose `mode` is `once` or `per_item` with the `series` it runs per item of (`lines.result`), and whose `msg` says it in English. A graph is compiled once, and how often each node runs is the same for every run of it, whatever a run is given. `graph.exclusive_groups`: each node's exclusive groups and their outputs.
- `graph.describe()`: the graph as an editor draws it, a `GraphDescription`: each node's fields as its hooks made them and how often it runs, the inputs, the outputs, the problems. Each input of a node says where it gets its value on each call of the node, its `source` (an `InputSource`: `mode`, `series` and `msg`): a `constant` (written in the record, or the default), a `graph_input` (the caller's), `one_value` (the output of a node called once), an `item` of a Series, an `outer_value` (returned outside the loop the node is inside) or `collected` (every item of a Series). A node with a problem is drawn with its fields all the same, and so is a node that reads it: an input whose edge is refused has the mode `missing`. A `type_mismatch` names that input in its `loc`; a `cycle` and `series_not_nested` name the node. Only a node whose fields aren't known has `found` false and no fields: an `unknown_node`, an `unknown_version`, an `invalid_node_id`, `subgraph_contains_itself`, a hook that failed or that wasn't called for a value it reads (`hook_needs_value`), a subgraph with problems of its own. Such a subgraph's inner nodes are not compiled into the graph: its problems are the graph's, each `loc` the subgraph node's id and then the place inside it (`("e", "x")`).
- Other codes: `unknown_node`, `unknown_version`, `unknown_input` (a value, default or edge naming an input the node lacks), `unknown_output` (an output, or a field of a record output, the node doesn't give), `type_mismatch`, `invalid_value` (a constant or default its type refuses), `duplicate_node_id`, `cycle`, `subgraph_contains_itself` (on the node that closes the circle), `hook_needs_value` (an input a hook reads has no constant), `parameter_name_invalid` (a hook gave a field a name no address can say).

### What a node returns

What a node returns is read strictly by its declared type: a value of exactly that class is taken as it is, a model may come back as a dict, but `"no"` is never a `bool`, `"12"` never an `int`, a date's text never a `date`, and `12.0` never an `int` column. `True` is never a number, wherever a value is read: an `int` or `float` input, an item of a list or a `Series`, a field of a `TypedDict`, a cell of a table (`bool_is_not_a_number`); the fields of your own pydantic model or dataclass are read by pydantic's rules. A fault fails that call of the node as `invalid_output` (`ctx`: `name`, `reason`, `errors`, a table's `column`), quoting nothing of the value. A value an edge carries that its source's type doesn't already guarantee fits (a limit on the input, an `int` into a `float`, a host type's own check) is read by the input as a constant is, and one it refuses is `invalid_edge_value` on the node it reached (`ctx`: `name`, `reason`, `errors`, a table's `column`). A table wired to a table input is checked when compiling, by each column the input declares whose type the source knows (`type_mismatch`, see "One or many"); a table of unknown columns is checked when it arrives.

### One or many

A node's types say how many values it deals with. `text: str` is one value. `Series[str]` is many values of one type, a series, each value an item. A `list[str]` and a table are each one value. In the quick start, `lines` returns a `Series[str]`, `upper` takes one text, and `join` takes a `Series[str]`. Each time conductor runs a node's function is one call; its result, an outcome, is what the run keeps.

- **A loop.** A `Series[T]` output wired to an input that takes one `T` starts a loop: that node is called once per item, each call with its own item, and so is every node downstream of it. Only a `Series` or `Table` input takes a series whole; every other input, an `Any` input included, takes it one item at a time. `graph.runs_on` says which series a node runs per item of.
- **A field of a record.** An edge may name one field of a record an output returns (a `TypedDict`, a pydantic model or a dataclass), one level down: `series-split.result.email`, on one record or on each item of a series of them. A field of a record of unknown fields is `Any` and is read when it arrives. A name the record lacks is `unknown_output`, listing its fields.
- **An outer value.** A value returned outside the loop a node is inside, by a node upstream of the series, is the same on every call: the document's name on each call for one of its lines. Nothing is copied.
- **Collect.** A `Series[T]` input wired to a node inside a loop collects the loop: it gets every `T` that node returned, in item order, and its own node is called once for all of them. Wired to a node called once, it gets that one value as a list of one. Where another input puts the node inside a loop itself (it also collects what was returned per line, so it runs per document), each call gets only what was returned for its own document, never every document's. A `Table[R]` input wired to records collects them into a table the same way; wired to a table, it takes that table, and wired to a `Series` of tables (a `Series[Table[R]]` output, or a table returned per item inside a subgraph) it takes one table per item, so its node runs once per item; a `Series[Table[R]]` input collects the tables. A bare `Table` input collects records of any columns: items that are a `dict`, a `TypedDict` or `Any` (a value declared `Any` is read as a table only where it is returned once in the graph, with no loop to collect; returned per item it is a record, so declare a table as one); a text, a number or any other value that is no record is `type_mismatch`, as it is into `Table[R]`. A `Series` output wired to a `Series` input passes whole.
- **Loops inside loops.** A node inside a loop may itself return a `Series`: each document has lines of its own, and the loop over the lines is inside the loop over the documents. A call's item indexes are one index per loop, outermost first: `(0, 3)` is the fourth line of the first document. Collecting ends the innermost loop only: a node that collects the lines runs once per document, and a node that collects that runs once.
- **Nested, or refused.** A node runs per item of the innermost series its inputs come from, and every other input comes from that series, from a series it is inside, or from outside them all. Items of two series that are not one inside the other never pair up: `series_not_nested`. Make one inside the other, by wiring the first into the node that returns the second (ten documents and three questions written in the graph: the node that returns the questions takes the document, so each document has its three questions), or give one of them whole to a `Series` input, where it is an outer value beside the other's items.
- **A table is one value.** It never starts a loop, and a column of it is no address. A node that returns `Series[R]` returns its records one item each; `series-split` in `syv-conductor-nodes` does that for any table or list. Such a node may return the records as a list or as the table itself: a table returned for `Series[R]`, `R` a `TypedDict`, is read as `Table[R]` is (its columns, each by its type, a `None` only where the type takes one) and kept by column, so an edge that names a field (`series-split.result.email`) reads the column and a node still receives plain `dict` records. A table returned for `Series[Any]` gives every column. Every field of a row type is required: a `NotRequired` field, or a `TypedDict` declared `total=False`, is refused when the node is declared (`row_field_optional`); declare it `X | None`, and a table with a column some rows leave out is not supported. A whole table or list wired to an input of one value is `type_mismatch` with `ctx.variant` `make_a_series` (`whole`, `fields`), and a field named on one is `unknown_output` with the same hint.
- A table fits a `Table[R]` input when it has every column `R` names, each of a type that fits; one it lacks is `type_mismatch` with `ctx.variant` `add_column` (`column`, `column_type`, `has`). A `Table[R]` input receives exactly the columns `R` names, whether the table was wired, given or collected. A `Table[R]` output is cut to `R`'s columns too; a bare `Table` output keeps every column it returns.
- A table written as the constant of a `Table` input, or given for one by a caller, is a frame or a list of records; `[]` is a table of no rows. Each column `R` names is read by its own type (a date from its ISO text, a host type from its own text), and other columns are left out. A missing column, or a cell its type refuses, is `invalid_value` as a constant and `invalid_input` when given, with `ctx.column` naming it.
- **Several edges into one input are alternatives,** for a `Series` input as for any other: each on its own branch of one node (outputs sharing an `exclusive_group`, or nodes downstream of them), so a call gets at most one; otherwise `several_edges_into_one_input`. They are inside the same loops, or `alternatives_from_different_loops`. Opposite branches into one `Series` input are collected as one list, in item order. Whole tables on opposite branches into one `Table` input are the one whose branch was chosen.
- **What collecting leaves out.**
  1. A `Series` input gets the items that have a value, in order. An item with none (`None`, or its branch not chosen) is left out of every `Series` input of the node together, so two `Series` inputs wired to one loop stay paired; `Series[T | None]` keeps its place as `None`. A `Series` output passed whole lines up with them the same way. A `Table` input keeps no place: a record is never `None`. No items is an empty list, and the node is called with it. Two `Series[X]` inputs wired to opposite branches of one node would lose every item: `lists_from_different_loops`.
  2. Only what was decided per item is left out. Before any item is looked at, the collecting node asks one question of what is decided outside the loop: could any item have a value here? The answers are ordered, skipped < `None` < could have a value. An outer value is read as it is. A node inside the loop is the worst of its inputs, where an input that takes `None` receives it; an input is the best of its alternative edges; an output in an `exclusive_group` of a node that isn't called is skipped. When no item could have a value, the collecting node is treated as any node wired there, with two items as with none: skipped when it is for a branch not chosen, not called when it is for a `None`. `Series[T] | None` then receives `None`, and `Series[T | None]`, which takes `None` per item, is called with a `None` in each item's place. A series that was never returned has no item, so it is the input's own `None`, and a node that chooses a branch from an item of it chooses none, which skips what collects that branch; downstream of a node that takes `None`, the choosing node could be called, so what collects its branch isn't called, as for any `None`. A list of one is read the same way: its one value, `None` or not, is its one item. When an item could have a value, each item answers for itself by rule 1: a branch chosen per item, or a `None` item, leaves only that item out.
  3. A collecting node waits until every item has an outcome.
- `SKIPPED` for one item leaves a gap there (`None` in `run.results`), and the nodes wired to it are skipped for that item; outside a loop it skips the nodes wired to it.
- `graph.run(max_items=1000)` is an item limit: the most items any one series a loop runs over may have, checked when the series is returned and before any call for its items. A series that is only collected or passed whole is not counted. Over it the run stops (`status` `stopped`) with the problem `item_limit` (`series`, `items`, `max_items`), and `run.with_max_items(...).resume()` goes on with a higher one, calling nothing again.
- A subgraph's inner nodes are inside every loop its node is inside, and a `Series` input inside it collects only loops inside the subgraph.

### Asking a person

`run.resume()` calls every node that is ready, until the run is complete, waits for a person, fails or is stopped, and returns the `Run`; `graph.run` does the same from the start. `status` says how it stopped (`complete`, `waiting`, `failed`, `stopped`, `cancelled`, `timed_out`), with `cause`, a `Problem`, for the last four. A node raises `Ask(prompt, choices=, default=)` and says so with `asks=True` on its `@node`: what is asked is what the node returns, so its return type says the answer's shape and how to ask, and how a question looks (title, description, widget) is its `Param`, as for an input. `-> str` with a bare `raise Ask(prompt)` is a free-text question. That call and every call downstream of it wait, the rest of the graph runs on, and the run ends `waiting`:

```python
@registry.node("approve", title="Approve", description="Asks a person whether to approve an invoice.", asks=True)
def approve(invoice: str) -> bool:
    raise Ask(f"Approve {invoice}?")


approving = Graph.compile(make_graph(approve, constants={"approve.invoice": "INV-1"}), registry)
paused = approving.run()                                 # paused.status == "waiting"
answered = paused.answer(paused.waiting[0], True)        # raises here if wrong; no node runs
finished = answered.resume()
again = Run.from_json(finished.to_json(), approving)           # a run is JSON
```

- One rule covers every question: a function that raises `Ask` is answered with a value of its return type. A node that raises it in its own function says `asks=True`, and the answer is its outputs; the node is not called again for that call. A raise from a node's own function without `asks=True` fails the call as `ask_not_declared`, so `describe().asks` is certain for every node: whether a call may wait for a person, which a host needs to know before running a graph unattended.
- A parameter may be the question instead, when the outputs are more than the answer: `def pay(invoice: str, ok: Annotated[bool, Asked(approval)]) -> str`, where `approval(invoice: str) -> bool` returns a value or raises `Ask`. The node is called once, with `ok` the function's return value (read by `ok`'s type, else `invalid_asked_value`) or the person's answer. The function's parameters are the node's, by name: its inputs, and its `Context` parameter when it takes one. It returns the parameter's type. No edge or constant reaches the parameter (`unknown_input`): `describe()` lists it as `asked`, not among `inputs`. A node has at most one, has no `asks=True` beside it, and the parameter has no default; each fault is a `NodeDeclarationError` (`asked_twice`, `asked_and_asks`, `asked_with_default`, `asked_not_on_a_parameter`, `asking_function_parameter_unknown`, `asking_function_returns_another_type`, `async_run`). Its waiting call has one question, the parameter's, answered with its value. The answer is saved with the run until the node is called with it; the call is then `answered`, and a later `run.again` reuses it as it reuses any answer, once each, in item order. An answer given and not yet used is not carried to a run of changed inputs (`with_inputs`, `again`, `forget`): that call asks again. The waiting id is made from all the node's inputs and the code of both functions, so a change to any input, or to either function, asks again.
- The return type says how to ask: `bool` a yes or no, `Literal["low", "high"]` one of its values, `str`, `int`, `float`, `date` a value, a frozen dataclass a form of one question per field (a field's default is proposed; one whose default is `SKIPPED` proposes nothing, and left out of the answer is a branch not chosen), `Table[R]` a table answered as records (read as a caller's table is, but each cell strictly from its JSON form: other columns are dropped and a missing column is refused), `Series[X]` several, so `Series[Literal[...]]` or `Series[str]` with `choices` is a pick of several. A hook's output types ask the same way.
- `Ask` adds what only the run knows. On one question (a node of one output, or an `Asked` parameter): `choices=[...]` (each a value, or `Choice(id, title)` to give it a title) and `default=`. Each has the answer's shape, so on several outputs each goes by output name: `choices={output: [...]}`, `default={output: value}`. An `Ask` that doesn't fit the outputs (a default or choice its type refuses, a default an answer couldn't be, no choices or one offered twice, a name that isn't an output, choices on a table, the one-output form on several or the several-output form on one) fails the node: `invalid_ask`, with `ctx.reason`.
- Each entry of `run.waiting` is a `Waiting`: `id` (`approve@1~3fa2c0d1`: the node's id, then `@` and a number for each item it was called for, from the outside in, `approve` alone for a node that runs once, then `~` and a fingerprint of the question asked there), `loc` (the node, then its item, as a problem's `loc`), `prompt`, `inputs` (what the call received, as JSON) and `questions`, one per output (one for an `Asked` parameter, the parameter's): the field record `describe()` writes (`name`, `title`, `is_series`, `type`, `schema`, `required`, ...; a lone output is titled by its own label, as `describe()` shows it: `Param(title=)` on the return type, else "Result"), with `choices` (`[{"id", "title"}]`, from the `Ask`, else the output's `Param(choices=)` or `Literal`) and `default` (from the `Ask`, else the output's own).
- `run.answer(waiting, value)` answers one waiting call; `run.answer({waiting_id: value, ...})` answers several in one call. It returns a new run, and nothing runs until `resume()`.
  - One question is answered with its value, several (a node of several outputs) with a mapping by output name. In the mapping, a question with a default may be left out, and so may one whose type takes `None` and that has no choices. Of an `exclusive_group`, exactly one is answered; the others are branches not chosen.
  - Each answer is read strictly from its JSON form: `true`, not `"yes"` or `1`; `3`, not `"3"`; a date as its ISO text. It is checked against its question before anything runs.
  - Every fault is refused at once, and nothing is answered: `invalid_answer` (`ctx.waiting_id`, `ctx.reason`, and `ctx.question` when it is about one), `not_waiting` for a call that is not waiting, and `answer_stale` (`ctx.current`, the id waiting there now) for an id whose call has asked another question since, as after `run.again` moved the items.
  - An id without its `~` part names the call alone and answers whatever question waits there. A node that asked is not called again for that item.
- `run.to_json()` is the whole run, a saved run. A table that two outputs share is written once: after a node `people` returns a table and `split` splits it, the save has the table under `outcomes.people.outputs.result`, `[null]` under `outcomes.split.outputs.result`, and `"tables_written_once": [{"output": ["split", "result", 0], "same_as": ["people", "result", 0]}]` (node, output, call number). A `null` in an output's list with an entry in that list means "this table is the one at that place"; reading the saved run gives both outputs the one table again. It names the graph it is of by `graph.fingerprint`: the record's nodes, versions, values, defaults and edges, not `display`.
- `Run.from_json(saved, graph)` refuses a saved run of another graph as `saved_run_of_another_graph`: an edited graph starts a new run, and `edited.with_inputs(..., previous=old_run)` reuses the old run's outcomes for the nodes the edit left as they were. Then it reads the saved run back and checks it against the graph: a saved run that doesn't fit it, or isn't a saved run at all, is `saved_run_unreadable`, with `ctx.where` saying where (`outcomes.upper.outputs.result.1`) and `ctx.reason` why. Every value is read back by its declared type. A float that isn't finite is written as its text (`"NaN"`, `"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"`): a `float` reads the float back, and `Any`, a `dict` or `float | str` reads the text, as a date under `Any` comes back as its ISO text.
- A saved run is one JSON text that a host stores and never reads or edits. It has the inputs, the outcome of each call of each node (its outputs, each written by the output's type; a question still waiting; an answer to an `Asked` parameter not yet used; not called for a `None`; skipped), the reusable outcomes from a previous run, and how the last `resume()` ended. Only nodes that were called are in it, so a long graph waiting at its start saves small, and it reads back from a store that reorders keys, such as Postgres `jsonb`. A `Series` of records a node returned as a table is saved as that table.
- A value with no JSON form is `run_unwritable` at `to_json`, naming where too. A node that asks a person on inputs with no JSON form fails as `question_unwritable`, naming the input: a question carries what its node received.
- The run's context is one object of a class the host names once, `NodeRegistry(context_type=X)`, passed to every call that starts or goes on with a run: `graph.run(context=X(...))`, `run.resume(context=...)`, `run.stream(context=...)`, `run.again(context=...)`. A node takes it as its first parameter, `def sign(ctx: Context[X], text: str)`, recognised by `Context`, not by its name; anywhere else, inside `| None`, a list or an output, `Context` is `context_misplaced`, and it names a class (`context_not_a_class`). A test calls `sign(context, "Done")`. The parameter is no input. A node names the registry's class, a base of it, or a `Protocol` whose members the class has (declare each as a read-only property, or a frozen dataclass does not satisfy it): that is how a node that doesn't know the host's class asks. Compiling checks it: a node asking for what the class is not or lacks, or for a context on a registry that names none, has `context_does_not_fit` at `(node_id, parameter)`, through the subgraph node for a node inside one. A run is refused at its start for a context that is not an instance of the class (`invalid_context`), and for none while a node takes it (`context_missing`, at each such node). A graph none of whose nodes takes it runs with one or without. `add_subregistry` takes a registry that names the same class or none, else `context_type_differs`. `NodeRegistry(context_type=X)` is a `NodeRegistry[X]`, its graphs `Graph[X]` and their runs `Run[X]`, so a type checker refuses a `context=` of another class; it cannot see that a graph's nodes need one. The context is never saved with a run.

### Running again

`run.again(**changed)` runs with changed inputs, the rest as before, and reuses what it can (`run.with_inputs(**changed)` is the same run not started, to `resume()` or `stream()`, as `graph.with_inputs` is to `graph.run`): a call that would get the same arguments as a call of the same node in the previous run reuses that call's outcome, even if its item moved, and the node isn't called. Answers are reused the same way.

```python
@registry.node("send", title="Send", description="Sends a message to a contact.")
def send(contact: str) -> str:
    return f"sent to {contact}"


sending = Graph.compile(make_graph(lines, send), registry)
first = sending.run(text="ida@a.dk\nbo@b.dk")                # two mails
second = first.again(text="ida@a.dk\nbo@b.dk\neva@c.dk")     # one contact added: one mail
```

- The key is what the call is about to receive, by content, plus the node's version, its code (the function's own bytecode and constants, as a saved run records it), its fields and the Series it runs per item of. The run's context is not part of it.
- A call reuses the outcome of the call with the same item indexes when that call got the same arguments; otherwise of any call of the node in the previous run that got the same arguments. So identical items share one previous outcome, and a further identical item reuses it too.
- A person's answer, or a question still waiting, is taken once and in item order: of the items that get the same arguments, the first takes the first previous answer and the second the second, whatever thread finished first, and an item beyond the answers there were is asked. It is reused only inside the same outer items, so two documents' identical lines keep each document's answers when the documents move. A question still waiting goes on waiting at its item's new place, asked nothing new.
- `again` passes on the reusable outcomes the run before it had and didn't use, while their node still has a question waiting, so an answer survives an edit and its revert; when a node is complete, the unused ones are dropped, so an edit undone two runs later calls the node for that item again.
- `run.forget("node", ...)` is a run of the same inputs that calls those nodes again (a subgraph node's id forgets its inner nodes), and a node downstream that then gets the same arguments as before is reused: a host checks access again this way.
- `Policy(reuse_when_inputs_match=False)` is for a node whose result depends on the world, not its inputs (a file read by its path, today's exchange rate): `again` calls it for every item.
- `node_complete.reused` says how many calls were reused.

### Retries and Timeouts

Retries live on the node's `Policy`, and count per call.

- Only `ExternalError` retries: raised by the node, or a class in `Policy.retry_on` (`external_failed`). Anything else is `execution_failed` or the node's own `NodeError` code, run once. A `NodeError` other than `ExternalError`, an `invalid_output` and an `Ask` are never retried, even when `retry_on` names a class they derive from, such as `Exception`.
- Attempt `n` waits `retry_delay * 2 ** (n - 1)` and emits `node_retry`.
- `Policy.attempt_timeout` bounds one attempt: the call fails with the code `timeout`, final; the thread is not interrupted, so the call runs on and the process waits for it at exit.
- `run.resume(timeout=60)` ends the run `timed_out` when that call of `resume()` takes longer (a `timeout` or `checkpoint_every` that is not a finite number of seconds above 0, a `bool` included, is `invalid_timeout` or `invalid_checkpoint_every` at the call, and a `max_items` of `True` is `invalid_max_items`); `run.stream(cancel=asyncio.Event())` ends it `cancelled` when set, and so does leaving the loop once the stream is closed: Python closes an async generator left early only when it is collected, so hold it with `async with contextlib.aclosing(run.stream()) as events:` and loop over `events`. Either way the calls already made finish and are kept, so resuming repeats none of them. `run.stream(hand_back=asyncio.Event())` stops calling nodes the same way and leaves the run going, for a host that shuts down and lets another process go on: the last event is then a `run_checkpoint` whose `run` is `running` and has the outcome of every call the stream waited for, and there is no `run_end`, since the run didn't end. A `cancel` set as well wins.

### Errors

The classes are exported from `conductor`. What is wrong is always one record, `Problem(type, loc, msg, ctx)`: on `graph.problems`, on `node_failed` and an ended run's `run.state`, and in `InvalidCallError.errors()`. Its `type` is a stable code (see "Problem and error codes"); a node failure's `loc` is `(node_id, *item_indexes)`, a graph problem's `(node_id, input)`.

```
NodeDeclarationError    a node or registry declared wrong, at import; a TypeError, with code and problem (DECLARATION_PROBLEMS)
InvalidCallError        a call was given what it cannot act on, every fault listed
NodeError               a node's own failure: message, code, ctx (JSON values only; anything else is pydantic's ValidationError where it is raised)
└── ExternalError         retried
```

A failed call ends the run `failed`, its problem the `cause` of `run.state`, an `EndedEarly`: nothing more starts, the calls already on a thread are waited for (each as far as its `attempt_timeout`) and kept, so resuming doesn't repeat them. A call that can't be acted on raises `InvalidCallError`, whose `errors()` lists a `Problem` for every fault, and nothing changes. Running a graph with problems raises it too, listing them. A failure never quotes a value the run handled: a node's exception other than a `NodeError` goes to `logging.getLogger("conductor")` and only its class name reaches `ctx`.

### Events

`async for event in run.stream():` yields frozen models from `conductor.events`, the union `Event` on `type`; the call is checked before anything is yielded. `run_start` is always first and `run_end` always last, but for a run handed back (`hand_back=`), whose stream ends with a `run_checkpoint`. The nodes are called on a thread of the run's own, so a slow node never blocks the event loop. `run_end` writes `status` and `cause`, the run's `Problem` when it failed, stopped, was cancelled or timed out (`null` otherwise), so a client sees why the run stopped (an `item_limit` cause carries `items` and `max_items`): `event.run` is for the host to save, and has every value; no event carries a node's values. An event writes itself as JSON: `event.model_dump(mode="json")`.

| Event | Carries |
|---|---|
| `node_start`, `node_skipped` | `loc`: the node's id, behind the id of each subgraph's node it is inside, `("emb", "upper")` |
| `node_progress` | `loc`, `finished`, `total` (`None` until every item exists); at most four a second per node |
| `node_complete` | `loc`, `outcomes` (how many calls it had), `not_called` (how many of them were not called for a `None`), `reused`; the values are in the run (`run.results`) |
| `node_retry` | `loc` (the call's: the node's id, then its item indexes; inside a subgraph the subgraph node and its index first, `("emb", 1, "upper")`), `attempt`, `retries`, `delay`, `cause` |
| `node_failed` | `loc`, `cause` (a `Problem`, whose `loc` names the call) |
| `node_waiting` | `waiting` (a `Waiting`) |
| `run_start` | `waiting` |
| `run_checkpoint` | `run` (status `running`, or how the run stopped), which it does not write; only with `stream(checkpoint_every=seconds)`, at most that often and once when the run is stopped with calls on threads; and as the last event of a run handed back (`stream(hand_back=)`), `running`, in place of `run_end` |
| `run_end` | `status`, `cause`, and `run`, which it does not write |

### Saving a graph

Records are frozen pydantic models. `GraphRecord` and `Problem` round-trip through JSON; a `Run` writes itself with `to_json()` and reads back with `Run.from_json`.

```python
record = make_graph(upper, join)
text = record.model_dump_json()
assert GraphRecord.model_validate_json(text) == record
```

### The Palette

A function node's `describe()` is a `FunctionNodeDescription`, a pydantic record (`kind` is `"function"`, `id`, `version`, `versions`, `title`, `description`, `category`, `tags`, `extra`, `docs`, `deprecation`, `policy`, `inputs`, `outputs`, `takes_added_inputs`, `computes_outputs`, `asks` (whether a call may wait for a person), `asked` (the `Asked` parameter's field, else `None`)); a subgraph is a `SubgraphDescription` (`kind` is `"subgraph"`, the same keys without `policy`, `takes_added_inputs`, `computes_outputs`, `asks` and `asked`). Each field is a `FieldDescription`, one flat record (`name`, `title`, `description`, `is_series`, `type`, `type_variables`, `json_schema` written as `schema`, `required`, `default`, `choices`, `widget`, `exclusive_group`; `type` and `schema` are always set, a table's columns are in both, as `Table[name: str]` and as a `columns` array in the schema; a key it doesn't have is `None`; a `Param`'s limits are in `schema`, as `minimum`, `maxLength` and the like, and its title and description are the field's own, never repeated there). `registry.describe()` is a `RegistryDescription`: `nodes` and `types` (each `id`, `title`, `accepted_as`). A subgraph's palette entry lists the fields it offers only in `registry.describe()`, which has the nodes its graph uses; a subgraph's definition has no `describe()`. `graph.describe()` is a `GraphDescription`: each input of a node is the `FieldDescription` as `field` beside its `source`, and each `GraphInputDescription` has the field as `field` beside its `address` and `node_id`. Each is a host's response model as it is; `model_dump(mode="json")` writes it.

## API Reference

Five public modules: `conductor`, `conductor.widgets`, `conductor.events`, `conductor.testing` and `conductor.about` (this reference, read with `python -m conductor.about`). Each but the last lists its names in `__all__`, and the list under each module below is written from it when this reference is read; import from nothing else.

### conductor

<!-- names: conductor -->

`NodeDefinition` is `FunctionDefinition | SubgraphDefinition`, `NodeDescription` is `FunctionNodeDescription | SubgraphDescription`, `RunState` is `Going | EndedEarly`, and `RunStatus` is every status a run can have.

`NodeRegistry(*, category="", tags=(), extra={}, types=(), context_type=None)` has `@registry.node`, `add(*definitions)`, `replace(definition)`, `remove(node_id)`, `add_subregistry(registry)`, `filter(predicate)`, `subgraph(...)`, `upgrade(record, node_id, to=None)`, `in`, `[]`, `len`, iteration over the definitions, `types`, `context_type`, `describe`. A node entering a registry takes its defaults: tags add up, outermost first; the node's own `category` and `extra` keys win. A second node under one id raises; a subregistry is copied in when added.

### Running

- `graph.run(inputs={}, /, *, max_items=None, context=None, timeout=None, **by_name)`: calls every node that is ready, from the start, until the run is complete, waits, fails or is stopped; its `Run`. A pause or failure is a `status`.
- `graph.with_inputs(inputs={}, /, *, max_items=None, **by_name)`: a `Run` with the inputs checked and not started; a name it doesn't offer (`not_offered`), a required one left out (`missing_input`), one given by both its name and its address (`input_given_twice`), a value its type can't read (`invalid_input`) or a `max_items` that is not a whole number of at least 1 (`invalid_max_items`; `True` and `2.5` are not) raises `InvalidCallError`, every fault at once.
- `run.resume(*, context=None, timeout=None, only_costs_nothing=False)`: goes on from where the run stopped, the same way. `run.stream(...)`, the same arguments and `cancel=`, `hand_back=`, `checkpoint_every=`: the same, yielding its events.
- `run.progress` (a `Progress`): how far the run is, read from its outcomes each time it is read, so a run read back with `Run.from_json` in another process has the same, and nothing of it is saved. For the run and for each node by node path as text (`nodes["shout"]`, `nodes["emb/upper"]`, a subgraph node the sum of the nodes inside it), a `CallCount`: `finished` (calls with an outcome that is not waiting: done, answered, skipped or not called), `waiting` (for a person), `known` (calls known so far: one per item of each series the node is looped over that exists; it only grows) and `total` (`None` while a series that decides it does not exist yet; the run's is `None` while any node's is). `total` counts calls, so a call skipped, not called or reused is counted. `Policy(costs_nothing=True)` marks a node whose call costs nothing and touches nothing outside the run (it hands on an upload, splits a table, returns a list given to it), and `run.resume(only_costs_nothing=True)` (or `stream`) calls only those, with the same `timeout`, events, `cancel` and checkpoints, and leaves the run `ready`: `graph.with_inputs(files=files).resume(only_costs_nothing=True).progress` gives every total the inputs decide before any call that costs something. A node behind a call that costs something stays `total: None` with `known` its floor; conductor does not guess. During it a call that raises (an `Ask` or a failure) has no outcome, and asks or fails at the next `resume()`; the item limit stops it as it stops any `resume()`. The next `resume()` makes none of its calls again and does not say again a node it completed. A node that takes `Context[...]` is refused `costs_nothing` (`costs_nothing_takes_context`).
- `run.with_max_items(n)`: the same run under another item limit, nothing started; a run `stopped` at its item limit goes on with `run.with_max_items(100).resume()`.
- `run.answer(waiting, value)` or `run.answer({waiting_id: value})`, `run.with_inputs(inputs={}, /, *, max_items=None, **by_name)` (a run that reuses this one's outcomes, to resume or stream), `run.forget(*node_ids)` (a run of the same inputs that calls these nodes again, reusing the rest, to resume or stream), `run.again(...)` (the same, resumed; takes `context=` and `timeout=` too), `run.to_json()`, `Run.from_json(saved, graph)`, `run.outputs_to_json()` (a complete run's `outputs` as JSON, each written by its output's type as a save writes it: a table as its columns, a float that isn't finite as its text, a host's type by its own schema; a value with no JSON form is `run_unwritable`, naming the output).
- `run.results`: every node's outputs so far, by node id: one value for a node that runs once, and for one that runs per item what a `Series` input wired to it would be given: a list in item order, `None` where an item has no value or no outcome yet, `[]` for a series returned with no items, and `None` in place of the list where no item could have a value, because the series was never returned: outside the loop there was a `None`, or a branch not chosen. Until the series is returned there is nothing so far, also `None`. So a host tells "nothing was tried" (`None`) from "tried, none" (`[]`). A node called per item of a list that is itself made per item shows a list of lists, with `None` for an outer item whose inner list was never made: three documents split into lines, the second empty, show `[["A", "B"], None, ["C"]]`, and `outputs_to_json` writes the same shape. `run.outputs`: narrowed to `graph.outputs`, by address, on a `complete` run only (`run_not_complete` otherwise). `run.waiting` (each a `Waiting`), `run.not_called` (each a `NotCalled`: `loc`, `input`), `run.status`, and `run.state`: `Going(status)` while nothing has ended it early (`ready`, `running`, `waiting`, `complete`), else `EndedEarly(status, cause)` (`failed`, `stopped`, `cancelled`, `timed_out`), read with `match run.state: case EndedEarly(cause=cause): ...`. A save keeps the status and, on an ended run, its cause; one whose status and cause disagree is `saved_run_unreadable`.

### Problem and error codes

A `Problem`'s `type` is a stable code, and a host translates by it, filling its sentence from `ctx`. `PROBLEMS.codes` is every code conductor itself writes, for a test that pins your translations to it; `DECLARATION_PROBLEMS` holds the codes of a `NodeDeclarationError`, which only a node's developer meets. A code that isn't in it is a node's own, from a `NodeError`. `python -m conductor.about problems` prints every code, the declaration codes and `check_registry`'s among them, each with its message, an example, what its `ctx` keys mean and how to fix it.

A kind of problem is declared once, by a function of a `ProblemCatalogue`, and `PROBLEMS` is the catalogue of conductor's core. Each kind has its `code`, its `variant` (what `ctx.variant` says when a code has a second message for one mistake), its `sentence` (the message with a placeholder for each `ctx` value), its `section` (where a host meets it) and `ctx_type`, a `TypedDict` of the keys its `ctx` has. A key that may be left out is absent when it does not apply, never `null`. A problem whose sentence names its node or field has them in `ctx` as `node_id` and `field`, so a sentence is filled from `ctx` alone. A `Problem` read from JSON is read as it is, whatever its code: a host that wants `ctx` typed validates it itself with pydantic, against the kind's `ctx_type`. A node may raise `NodeError(code=...)` under a code that is also in the catalogue; conductor leaves it, so that problem carries the node's `ctx` under the catalogue's code. `python -m conductor.about <code>` prints one, as `python -m conductor.about context-missing`.

### conductor.widgets

Frozen models with a `type`, and a host subclasses `Widget` for a control of its own; compiling and running never read one. `title`, `description` and the limits of a value (`ge`, `gt`, `le`, `lt`, `multiple_of`, `min_length`, `max_length`, `pattern`) belong to the `Param`, and a value outside its limits is refused. An untitled field reads as its name in everyday words. No type has a default widget. A `Param`'s widget is a `Widget`; a type checker refuses a class passed bare.

<!-- names: conductor.widgets -->

### conductor.testing

<!-- names: conductor.testing -->

`check_registry(registry, /, *, examples={}, context=None)` is one test a node package or host runs in CI: `assert check_registry(registry, examples={"upper": [{"text": "hi"}]}) == []`.

- It returns every problem at once as `Problem`s, `loc` `(node_id, version)`. For `example_for_no_node` given without a version, `loc` is `(node_id,)`.
- A body is called only for a node given an example, once per example, through the engine as a graph of that one node. `(id, version)` keys an older version's examples, and `context=` gives every example the run's context, as `graph.run` takes it.
- The checks are `hook_failed`, `needs_example`, `upgrade_broken`, `changed_its_inputs`, `run_failed` and `example_for_no_node`; `python -m conductor.about problems` says what each means and how to fix it. These codes are `check_registry`'s, not in `PROBLEMS.codes`.
- A node known to fail goes in a test of its own marked `pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True)`, checking `registry.filter(...)` down to it (`python -m conductor.about run-failed` shows one).


### conductor.events

Every event record, and `Event`, their union on `type`:

<!-- names: conductor.events -->

## Serving Runs

The core has no HTTP in it. `syv-conductor-providers` has `conductor_providers.fastapi.run_router(store=, registry=, caller=, may_see=)`, a FastAPI router mounted with `app.include_router(...)`: `GET /nodes`, `POST /compile`, `POST /estimate` (the body of `POST /runs`; `resume(only_costs_nothing=True)` with the caller's context, answering `run.progress` and storing nothing), and a run you start, follow, read (with its `progress`, as of its last checkpoint while it runs), answer, resume, run again and cancel by id, from any worker; `docs/serving-runs.md` is its guide. The host writes the `conductor_providers.fastapi.RunStore`, six async methods over one row per run (`conductor_providers.fastapi.StoredRun`: ten columns, of which a store acts on `id`, `rev`, `owner` and `lease_until`, a host queries `status` and `caller`, and `graph`, `run`, `state` and `outcome` are the router's JSON, kept as text) whose every change is a compare-and-set on `rev` (`await conductor_providers.fastapi.testing.check_run_store(store)` returns every way a store differs from what the router relies on, as problems), and a FastAPI dependency for the caller, a class or a function with a return annotation, whose type is kept on each run. With a `caller`, `may_see(caller, started_by)` is required and says who may read and act on a run; there is no default, and the caller should hold what identifies them and nothing that changes, since a run keeps its caller as they were when it started. `registry=` may be a function of the caller, for a registry per tenant. `context=` is a function of the caller that returns the run's context, an instance of the registry's `context_type`, called each time a run is resumed. A node is given a way to connect, never a connection, because it runs on another thread. An answer claims the run at the revision it read. A lease, renewed while the run is running, lets another worker resume a dead worker's run from its last `run_checkpoint`. A deploy hands its runs back (`stream(hand_back=)`), each run stored as it is, still `running`. Answers sent while a run is running wait on the run and are applied when it stops. Every refusal the router makes is `{"detail": [problem, ...]}`: a 422 has the codes of the graph or the run, a 404 and a 409 the router's own (`no_such_run`, `already_answered`, `run_complete`, `run_not_resumable`, `run_changed`); a run whose worker raised outside a node while resuming it ends `failed`, with conductor's own problem as the cause where conductor refused to resume it (`context_missing`, `invalid_context`, `saved_run_unreadable`, `run_unwritable`) and `resume_failed` otherwise, and the run lists what waits in its last checkpoint; a raise from the store fails no run, and once the lease runs out another worker goes on with it; a queued answer whose type's check raises is refused as `answer_check_failed`; `conductor_providers.fastapi.ROUTER_PROBLEMS` is the catalogue of the router's seven codes, read as `PROBLEMS` is.

```
packages/
└── conductor/src/conductor/            __init__, widgets, events, testing, about: the five public modules
    ├── about/                          this document
    └── _internal/                      everything else; import nothing from here
```

```bash
python -m conductor.about                 # full text
python -m conductor.about sections        # section slugs
python -m conductor.about one-or-many     # one section (prefix or substring)
```
